idiom_name: generic one-liner function identity<T>(x: T): T { return x; }
implementation_notes: TypeScript has no identity function in its own standard library; the classic structure collapses into a one-line generic function, function identity<T>(x: T): T { return x; }, whose type parameter traffics the argument type to the return type so the output type equals the input type (the Handbook's 'hello world of generics' — explicitly contrasted there with an any-typed version, which loses the type). The generic annotation is what makes the pattern type-preserving: const identity = <T>(x: T): T => x feeds Array.prototype.sort comparators, reduce base cases and RxJS pipe slots without casts. Canonical instances exist in libraries — RxJS exports identity<T>(x: T): T precisely to fill conditional operator slots (pipe(shouldLimit() ? take(5) : identity)), and lodash ships _.identity as its default callback — so prefer importing one over redefining it. The classic form is still justified where a framework expects a unary transformer in a typed plugin/pipeline interface: a monomorphic (x: string) => string does not satisfy a (x: T) => T slot, and structural typing catches wrong-arity identities (a unary id offered where a binary comparator is expected) at compile time — where plain JavaScript would fail silently at runtime.
pitfalls: Annotating the parameter as unknown instead of a type parameter — const identity = (x: unknown) => x — compiles but returns unknown, breaking inference at every call site; the generic <T>(x: T) => T is required to keep the type.
In .tsx files the arrow generic <T>(x: T) => x is parsed as JSX and is a syntax error; write function identity<T>(x: T): T, or <T,>(x: T) => x, or <T extends unknown>(x: T) => x.

const identity = (x: any) => x 'works' but is the any-typed version the Handbook warns about: it silently erases the return type and spreads any downstream, defeating the pattern's type-preservation guarantee.

tsc emits unoptimized JavaScript: unless the bundler/minifier inlines it, a fresh arrow (x) => x allocated per call site in a hot loop costs real closures — hoist one module-level const identity and pass it by reference.

identity preserves null and undefined — it returns exactly what it is given and is not a nullish guard; code that must distinguish 'absent' from 'present' needs T | undefined and nullish checks, not identity.
As a promise catch handler, identity 'handles' the rejection by resolving with it, so missing error handling looks like success — errors propagate unchanged and unreported.
